US ADP Employment Change Oct: 86K (est 75K; prev 90K; prev R 86K)

ADP’s private payroll count beat again in October, and two straight 86K months have pulled the three-month average back up to 69K from 55K, its first increase since June. That’s 16 straight monthly gains, and 2026 is now averaging 71K a month against 29K over the same stretch of 2025.

▪️ The lead changed hands: trade/transport +39K was the most since January 2025 and ended education/health’s 12-month run on top (+28K, its least since July 2025)
▪️ Professional/business services −27K, a third straight decline and the worst since February, now −118K year to date
▪️ All five firm-size tiers added jobs for a second month, and unusually evenly (500+ at +24K, 50–249 at +22K, 1–19 at +21K)
▪️ The South (+47K) and West (+28K) carried it, while the Northeast gave back its September surge (+3K after +63K)

The pay detail was another story. 

Job-changers’ gross pay growth hit 7.6%, the fastest since March 2024. That widened their premium over job-stayers (4.4%, an eighth flat month) to 3.2 points, the widest since August 2023.  ADP’s Nela Richardson says switchers were “lured by a combination of bonuses, overtime, and more hours in addition to higher base pay.”  That fits with Tuesday’s JOLTS, where quits hit their highest since March 2025.

Note: On ADP’s base-pay measure, changers are only at 4.8%, so the extra money is coming through bonuses and hours rather than wage rates.

Treasury’s Quarterly Refunding announcement is out, setting auction sizes for the upcoming quarter. The sizes came in as expected, but the long end jumped on the release before settling back.

In terms of auction sizes, Treasury kept note and bond sizes unchanged at $125B for next week’s refunding (3s, 10s, 30s). So there was no cut to 20- and 30-year bonds, which some, including Citi, had expected this month. It also repeated that it sees “strong demand” for bills.

However, the Treasury Borrowing Advisory Committee (TBAC) sounded less sure about that:

▪ Money market fund assets “have leveled off,” and the bill market “has started to show some signs of price sensitivity”

▪ It recommended larger coupon auctions in the second half of FY27 (April–September 2027), focused on 2- to 10-year notes, with “meaningful discussion” about future 20- and 30-year sizes

▪ Dealers see a $2.14T funding shortfall in FY28–29 at current auction sizes. Bills can cover FY27’s “modest” gap, but not that much

▪ TBAC said the maturity mix should be managed through auction sizes, not buybacks, even as Treasury nearly doubled its planned liquidity buybacks to up to $70B this quarter, from $38B in August’s plan

Treasury also softened its guidance to holding sizes “for the next several quarters,” dropping “at least.” Starting in March 2027, the 7-year note moves to a new issue each quarter with two reopenings.

Per Claude’s calculations, bills could reach close to 24% of marketable debt by March, the highest since late 2020. The Fed has already hiked once, and markets price about three more increases over the coming year (per TBAC). If bill buyers also start demanding higher yields, it’s a double whammy for Treasury’s interest costs.

Given concerns about what a Democratic “Blue Wave” would mean for the AI trade, predictably tech fell as early returns showed just that, with Nasdaq-100 futures down about 1.5% at midnight. But it appears traders are rethinking it with those futures now trading slightly higher and the SPX indicated up nearly 1%.

That may be in part because the first read from most analysts is that the sweep slows the AI data center buildout rather than stops it.

In the third-quarter Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey (SLOOS), banks reported that business loan demand weakened for the first time since the second quarter of 2025. But other data doesn’t show businesses borrowing less.

The Fed’s weekly bank lending data shows commercial & industrial (C&I) loans are up 11.3% year-over-year, the fastest since early 2023 (h/t Ed Yardeni), and we know equipment spending surged at a 20.9% annualized rate in third-quarter GDP.

The banks’ own explanation hints at what’s going on: “customer borrowing shifting to more attractive bank or nonbank funding sources.”

Worth noting, the survey’s demand reading has historically led actual C&I loan growth by about three quarters (correlation of 0.64 since 1991), so either loan growth cools into mid-2027 or the survey is off this time.

Interestingly, though, while banks left business loan standards little changed, they tightened standards on every type of loan to the nonbank lenders (nondepository financial institutions, or NDFIs) that may be taking their business:

▪️ Private credit (business credit intermediaries): a net 22% of banks tightened, while a net 10.7% saw stronger demand from them
▪️ Private equity funds: 15.4% tightened, demand up 5.4%
▪️ Mortgage and consumer credit intermediaries and other NDFIs: 16.7% to 20.4% tightened
Despite that, bank loans to NDFIs are up 20.3% year-over-year, about the 20% to 22% pace they’ve held all year. Meanwhile, loan-loss reserves are flat at $202 billion while total loans grew 7.9%, so coverage slipped to 1.42% of loans from 1.54% a year ago.

Some other nuggets from the SLOOS report:
▪️ Commercial real estate standards tightened in all three categories for the first time since the third quarter of 2024, with large banks flipping tighter after six straight surveys of easing on construction and multifamily loans
▪️ Mortgage demand weakened in all seven categories, while credit card demand was the strongest since the third quarter of 2022

I have not used technical analysis much in analyzing bond yields, but I've been hearing more and more of it so thought this Reuters article via @C_Barraud was interesting on the 10-year Treasury yield. 

It notes the yield had fallen four straight weeks through Friday to 4.91%, down from a 24-year intraday high of 5.36% on Oct. 7. It was 3.96% just before the Iran war began.

Reuters says it’s “too soon to say the rising trend that began with the Iran war is over.”

The key line they say is the rising 20-week moving average near 4.81%, which has halted pullbacks several times this year. Analysts aren’t likely to treat the slide as durable until the 10-year breaks below it and stays there.

If it breaks, support levels are:
▪ 4.75% to 4.68%
▪ ~4.62%
▪ 4.50% to 4.40%, the top of a symmetrical triangle, which also holds the 20-month moving average

If yields turn back up, resistance levels are:
▪ ~5.07%, the upper yearly Bollinger Band
▪ 5.16% to 5.18%
▪ 5.3645%, the Oct. 7 peak
▪ 5.48% to 5.52%, then the 50-year moving average near 5.65%

A move above 6% would bring 6.24% into view. That’s a Fibonacci retracement of the 1981 to 2020 decline in yields.

Advanced Micro Devices ($AMD) shares up 8% after a Q3 beat and guiding Q4 well above the Street on data center strength.

Third quarter vs. TipRanks consensus:
▪️ Non-GAAP EPS $2.09 vs. $1.95, up 74% from a year ago
▪️ Revenue $13.38B vs. $13.1B, up 45%, and $77M above the top of AMD’s own guide range
▪️ Data Center a record $8.55B, up 97%, vs. $8.2B expected per Bloomberg
▪️ Client $2.95B, up 7%, a hair under the $3.0B FactSet estimate
▪️ Gaming $773M, down 40% but well above the $634M estimate; Embedded $1.11B, up 29%

Fourth-quarter guide: $17B, plus or minus 3%, vs. $16.14B consensus. Even the low end beats by about $350M. The non-GAAP gross margin guide of about 55% though is down from 56%; StreetAccount was at 55.3%, per CNBC but markets seem to be looking past that.

Data Center added $4.2B, 102% of AMD’s $4.1B revenue increase. Everything else combined shrank 1.5%. Data Center now earns 74% of segment operating income on 64% of revenue, and its operating margin rose 9 points to 33.7%.

Some other quibbles:
▪️ Free cash flow fell 64% to $554M, about half the $1.05B expected and a 4% margin vs. 17% a year ago, as working capital absorbed $3.4B. The biggest piece was a $3.0B inventory build; inventory is up 45% since December to $11.5B.
▪️ No buybacks. AMD spent $1.5B withholding employee shares for taxes, 2.7 times free cash flow, and borrowed $4.7B.
▪️ GAAP EPS of $1.46 absorbed a $1.1B charge on warrants issued to customers. That liability rises with the share price.

The hyperscaler math: Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft and Meta spent $208.8B on capex last quarter. AMD’s Data Center revenue was 4.1% of that, so each point of share is worth about $2.1B a quarter.

To watch: fourth-quarter cash flow, inventory, and the margin step-down.
